title: Additional work examples
subtitle: Strategic Design Leadership Across Multiple Verticals

content.text: For the fashion vertical, I led design by grounding the work in clear, research-backed design principles. These weren't abstract ideas — they were aligned to Walmart's brand promise and distilled from customer insights. By codifying what mattered most to shoppers, the principles helped our cross-functional teams stay focused on customer value even as priorities shifted.

I drove the creation and adoption of these principles, making sure they weren't just a design artifact but a shared north star for product, engineering, and business partners. This elevated design's voice in strategic conversations and ensured execution always tied back to customer needs.
content.author: My role

content.text: One of the most effective ways to align teams is to paint a clear picture of the future. I facilitated design sprints and discovery projects that brought design, product, engineering, and business leaders together to imagine what our experience could look like beyond the next quarter.

I led the visioning process, ensuring we balanced imagination with feasibility. These efforts didn't just create inspiring concepts — they gave executives and teams a tangible vision to rally around, clarifying how near-term roadmaps fit into a longer journey.
content.author: My role

sections.title: Building a healthy pipeline of customer-driven features

content.text: In eCommerce fulfillment, my focus was on ensuring the team had a steady supply of features and goals grounded in research and discovery. Rather than reacting to short-term demands, we invested in understanding customer journeys and unmet needs, which allowed us to prioritize work with confidence.

I advocated for a balanced pipeline — ensuring design surfaced opportunities proactively while aligning with product and engineering on delivery. This made the roadmap more resilient and better tied to real customer impact.
content.author: My role

content.text: I championed journey mapping as a leadership tool, not just a design artifact. It became a way to advocate for the customer at every step, helping executives and teams see not only what we were building, but why it mattered to people in the real world.
